briefs.problem: There is no defined way to reliably identify and admit attendees at the venue entrance, or to produce a trustworthy record of who actually arrived.
briefs.solution: A staff-facing check-in app that identifies attendees at the door (scan plus manual fallback), records their arrival against an event attendee list, and produces an attendance record afterward.
introduces: an offline-capable local attendee snapshot with background sync to a central record
concurrency handling across multiple entrance devices scanning independently
a manual search / on-the-spot registration fallback for failed scans and walk-ins
a check-in data model distinguishing duplicate, re-entry, and multi-zone access
a post-event attendance export as a client deliverable

challenges.headline: Connectivity assumed, not confirmed
challenges.premise: The request describes 'staff check attendees in at the venue entrance' as if the device will always be online.
challenges.alternative: Treating offline capability as the default design assumption — local snapshot of the attendee list plus deferred, conflict-aware sync — protects the check-in path even if it turns out the venue has good wifi.
challenges.consequence: If connectivity is assumed and the venue has the patchy wifi event venues typically have, the check-in path can fail visibly in front of the client with no fallback, on a day that cannot be repeated.
challenges.recommendation: Settle the offline requirement before any architecture work starts, and if in doubt, build for offline as the safer default.

challenges.headline: 'Check in' is not one action
challenges.premise: The request treats check-in as a single boolean action per attendee.
challenges.alternative: Defining upfront whether a second scan means a blocked duplicate, an allowed re-entry, or a separate zone/session check-in lets the data model and the concurrency rule be designed once, correctly.
challenges.consequence: Building a naive boolean check-in first and retrofitting duplicate/re-entry/zone logic later touches the data model, the UI, and the sync layer all at once, under a date that cannot move.
challenges.recommendation: Resolve the check-in semantics and the concurrent-scan outcome with the client before the data model is fixed.

challenges.headline: One-off vs. reusable kit unresolved
challenges.premise: The request reads as a single-event build, but this is never stated.
challenges.alternative: Confirming scope now — one event or the first instance of a kit — lets configurability, the data model (single-event vs. multi-event), and cost be sized correctly from the start.
challenges.consequence: Building single-event and discovering later that reuse is expected means re-architecting the attendee/category/zone model and the configuration surface after the fact.
challenges.recommendation: Ask directly whether other events are planned before scoping or quoting.

briefs.cost_driver: the offline-capable sync and conflict-resolution layer across entrance devices
risks: The connectivity requirement is entirely unaddressed — building online-only and hitting a dead venue network on the day is the single biggest failure mode this context flags.
No defined outcome for simultaneous scans at different entrances means two devices admitting the same attendee twice is currently unhandled.
The attendee list's source and on-site correction path are unknown — if there's no way to add walk-ins or fix names at the door, the app breaks against real arrivals.
No success metric or throughput target is defined, so there is no way to validate the build is fast enough at peak arrival before the event day itself proves it.
A fixed, immovable date means any gap discovered late (offline, concurrency, fallback) cannot be fixed after the fact — it must be caught in rehearsal.

opportunities.text: If multiple events are confirmed, generalize the Event/Attendee/Category/Zone model and the check-in engine into a reusable kit rather than a one-off build.

Design the post-event attendance export now as a defined client deliverable (who came, when, where) rather than an ad hoc report assembled after the fact.

challenges.headline: One-off app vs reusable kit
challenges.premise: The request reads as a single app for one event, with no mention of future events.
challenges.alternative: Settling explicitly whether this is the first instance of a reusable event kit changes the data model (single-event vs multi-event), the configurability layer, and the pricing — it is cheaper to decide this before writing code than to retrofit it.
challenges.consequence: Building single-event assumptions into the data model now makes a later pivot to multi-event reuse a rebuild, not an extension.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client directly whether more events are planned before any architecture decision is made.

challenges.headline: Connectivity assumed reliable
challenges.premise: Nothing in the request addresses venue network conditions, implying an always-online check-in flow is acceptable.
challenges.alternative: Designing for a local attendee snapshot with check-ins queued and synced later removes the single point of failure that venue wifi and saturated 4G represent.
challenges.consequence: If the venue network degrades during the event's only few hours of use, an online-only app fails visibly in front of the client with no chance to fix it afterward.
challenges.recommendation: Test connectivity at the actual venue (or assume the worst) and commit to the offline-or-online architecture before building, since it drives the whole build differently.

challenges.headline: Check-in treated as one action
challenges.premise: "Check attendees in" is treated as a single scan-and-done action.
challenges.alternative: Explicitly defining what a second scan means — blocked duplicate, allowed re-entry, or access to a different zone/session — lets the data model and UI be built once instead of patched after the first real conflict.
challenges.consequence: A naive single-state check-in model breaks the first time someone re-enters or the event has multiple zones, which is a near-certainty per the event's own structure.
challenges.recommendation: Define the check-in semantics and whether zones/sessions exist before finalizing the data model.

decisions.decision: On-site staff, not attendees themselves, operate the check-in device.

exclusions.option: Building the full reusable, multi-event configurable architecture from day one
exclusions.reason: Whether this client will run more events at all is still unanswered; committing to that abstraction now, under a fixed and immovable event date, risks spending the available time on generality the client may never use.

exclusions.option: Building out the full post-event reporting/dashboard suite in this phase
exclusions.reason: The event date can't move and the core check-in path (identification, fallback, duplicate handling, offline resilience) is the one thing that must not fail on the day; reporting polish should not compete with it for the remaining time.

thresholds.condition: The venue connectivity test shows the network cannot be trusted during check-in hours
thresholds.measure: on-site network reliability test at the actual entrance(s)
thresholds.action: commit to an offline-first architecture (local snapshot + queued sync) rather than an online-only design

thresholds.condition: The client confirms they intend to run further events beyond this one
thresholds.action: invest in the configurable, reusable event-kit architecture instead of a disposable single-event build
